hint1: An exam word you often see with graphs, photos and maps.
hint2: Only say what happens. You don't need to say why.
hint3: Give a full picture in words, but no reasons.
hint4: '___ your bedroom to me: what's in it? What colour is it?'

hint1: Teachers do this at the board all day.
hint2: An exam word that wants more than describing.
hint3: Give causes, not only what happens.
hint4: 'You're late again! Can you ___?'

hint1: An exam task for two poems, two graphs or two cities.
hint2: Shoppers do this with prices before they buy.
hint3: Say how two things are like each other, and how they are not.
hint4: Parents shouldn't ___ their child with other kids.

hint1: A short exam task, often worth just one mark.
hint2: Pick out the right thing from a text or picture, nothing more.
hint3: Birdwatchers try to do this with every bird they see.
hint4: 'Can you ___ the man in this photo?' asks the police officer.

hint1: A short exam task: no full sentences needed.
hint2: Give three or four, one after another, with no detail.
hint3: Like identify, but with several things, often one per line.
hint4: 'Eggs, milk, bread' on a note before the supermarket.

hint1: An exam word where many different answers can get the mark.
hint2: Put forward one reason that could be true.
hint3: You do this when you say, 'How about pizza tonight?'
hint4: 'I ___ we take a taxi,' said Dad.

hint1: A command word often worth only two or three marks.
hint2: Give the key stages, without going into detail.
hint3: Less than describe, but more than a list.
hint4: Also a line drawn around the edge of a shape.

hint1: A top-level command word in Literature and Media essays.
hint2: Zoom in on techniques and their effects, piece by piece.
hint3: Break something into its parts and show how they work together.
hint4: Lab workers do this to a blood sample to see what is in it.

hint1: Often the highest-mark task on an exam paper.
hint2: Look at strengths and weaknesses using evidence.
hint3: Analysing alone won't do: decide how well it worked.
hint4: '___ the success of the policy.' End with a clear verdict.

hint1: Often comes right after 'Choose one' in an exam.
hint2: Make an examiner believe your decision was right.
hint3: Like 'explain', but for your own choice or opinion.
hint4: '___ your answer: why is this method the best?'

hint1: An essay task that looks at an issue from more than one angle.
hint2: Give the pros and cons of online learning, then your view.
hint3: Careful: it's never followed by 'about'.
hint4: '___ with your partner for two minutes,' says the teacher.

hint1: Many history essay titles begin with it.
hint2: It asks how much something is true, not just yes or no.
hint3: Good answers say 'largely', 'partly' or 'hardly at all'.
hint4: '___ do you agree with this statement?'

hint1: A very common joining word in answers.
hint2: It joins what happened to what made it happen.
hint3: Kids sometimes answer with only this word: '___!'
hint4: 'I am late ___ the bus didn't come.'

hint1: A tiny word that links two ideas.
hint2: It comes after the reason and before what happened.
hint3: 'It was raining, ___ we stayed at home.'
hint4: 'I'm ___ happy!' Here it means 'very'.

hint1: A short joining word, often after a comma.
hint2: It joins a good point and a bad point.
hint3: People say 'Yes, ___...' when they don't fully agree.
hint4: 'The phone is nice, ___ it is very expensive.'

hint1: You will see it many times in any essay.
hint2: Put it at the start of a new sentence, then a comma.
hint3: A more formal way to show a change of direction.
hint4: 'The method is cheap. ___, it is slow.'

hint1: A small word for when you have one more point.
hint2: Use it for your second or third point, not the first.
hint3: It usually goes just before the verb.
hint4: 'My dad speaks English. He ___ speaks French.'

hint1: A linker that makes a point easier to understand.
hint2: It helps you back up your point with a real case.
hint3: It comes just before you name one or two cases.
hint4: 'Some fruits are red, ___, strawberries and cherries.'

hint1: Maths and science reports use it a lot.
hint2: A formal word that leads to the logical next step.
hint3: 'The sample was small. ___, the data may not be reliable.'
hint4: 'I think, ___ I am,' said Descartes.

hint1: A linker you can put at the start of a sentence.
hint2: The second idea is a surprise after the first.
hint3: It joins two opposite ideas inside one sentence.
hint4: '___ it was raining, we went to the beach.'

hint1: A formal linker common in science and geography.
hint2: It sets two facts side by side to show how they differ.
hint3: Unlike 'although', there is no surprise, just a difference.
hint4: 'Cats are independent, ___ dogs need more attention.'

hint1: Often starts the second sentence in history or science answers.
hint2: It links one event to the effect it had.
hint3: Put it between the cause and the effect sentences.
hint4: 'Factories closed. ___, many people lost their jobs.'

hint1: Writers use it to build up an argument, point by point.
hint2: It brings in one more point, often a strong one.
hint3: It can come before 'to': '___ to the cost, it is slow.'
hint4: 'Solar power is clean. ___, it is getting cheaper.'

hint1: Very useful in 'for and against' essays.
hint2: It turns your essay towards the second view.
hint3: It often comes after 'On the one...' earlier in the paragraph.
hint4: 'Cars are convenient. ___, they cause pollution.'

hint1: Graphs, maps and photos all do this.
hint2: It makes a fact clear for everyone to look at.
hint3: On TV, a talent ___ or a cooking ___.
hint4: '___ me your homework, please,' says the teacher.

hint1: Doctors try to find this behind every illness.
hint2: It comes first in a chain of events and starts the rest.
hint3: Too much sugar can ___ bad teeth.
hint4: 'Smoking can ___ serious illness.'

hint1: The weather can do this to your mood.
hint2: Phones at bedtime can do this to your sleep.
hint3: People often mix it up with a noun that sounds the same.
hint4: 'Lack of sleep can ___ your exam results.'

hint1: Graphs about world population show this.
hint2: Prices in shops seem to do this every year.
hint3: On a line graph, the line climbs higher.
hint4: Your pocket money changes from 50 to 80 yuan.

hint1: Temperatures do this as autumn turns to winter.
hint2: The number of cars on the road does this at night.
hint3: On a line graph, the line drops lower.

hint1: Seasons do this four times a year.
hint2: You do this when you take off your uniform for PE.
hint3: The coins a shop gives back when you pay too much.
hint4: Leaves ___ colour in autumn.

hint1: Scientists use it to sound careful about their findings.

hint4: 'The results ___ that the medicine works, but we can't be sure.'

hint1: A formal verb in science reports.

hint3: 'The data ___ a link between diet and health.'
hint4: Drivers flash a light to ___ they are turning left.

hint1: Common in history answers about chains of events.
hint2: It connects one event to a later one it brings about.
hint3: 'This road ___ the beach.'
hint4: 'Too much screen time can ___ poor sleep.'

hint1: Quotes and data in your essay should do this.
hint2: Like table legs holding the top up.
hint3: 'These results ___ the theory.'
hint4: Fans do this for their favourite football team.

hint1: Lawyers do this in court for their client.
hint2: Give a case for your view, step by step.
hint3: Each team in a debate does this for its own side.
hint4: 'In this article, the writer ___s that school should start later.'

hint1: Governments try to do this to pollution.
hint2: Recycling does this to waste.
hint3: Shops do this to prices in a sale.
hint4: '___, reuse, recycle.'

hint1: Your teacher wants one when you are late.
hint2: People ask for one when you say no.
hint3: It comes before the result, not after.
hint4: 'Give me one good ___ to do my homework!'

hint1: Scientists write it down after a test.
hint2: It comes after the reason, not before.
hint3: After a football match, you check this: 2-1, 3-0.
hint4: Students wait for their exam ___s in summer.

hint4: 'A cat is an ___ of a pet.'

hint1: Maths homework is full of them.

hint3: If your phone won't turn on, you have one.

hint3: In an essay, quotes and data that back up your point.
hint4: In a PEE paragraph: Point, ___, Explain.

hint1: Students say this a lot when they share ideas.

hint1: Teachers draw a star next to notes like this.
hint2: A teacher says it about the parts that will be in the exam.

hint1: A calculator is this in a maths test.
hint2: An umbrella is this on a rainy day.
hint3: Something that makes a job easier is this.

hint1: A news story should be this.

hint1: In a debate, you do this with your own team.
hint2: People often nod their heads to show it.
hint3: Your friend says, 'Pizza is the best!' You say, 'Me too!'
hint4: 'I ___ with you. You are so right.'

hint1: Scientists sometimes do this about a new theory.
hint2: The two teams in a debate do this.
hint3: Your friend says, 'Maths is boring.' You say, 'Really? I love it!'
hint4: 'I ___ with you. I think you are wrong.'

hint1: Scientists use it for results that are unlikely to be just luck.

hint4: 'There was a ___ increase in sales this year.'

hint1: Advertisers want every advert to be this.
hint2: Doctors test new medicines to see if they are this.

hint4: 'Tests show that the new vaccine is highly ___.'

hint1: Good friends and good cars are both this.
hint2: Scientists repeat tests to make sure their results are this.
hint3: A bus that always comes on time is this.

hint1: Your school report lists these and also your targets.

hint4: Something you do really well, like drawing or maths.

hint1: Every argument has at least one, if you look closely.
hint2: Exam answers should look at the good points and these too.
hint3: Kryptonite is Superman's biggest one.
hint4: 'One ___ of the argument is the lack of evidence.'

hint1: Lawyers need this kind of argument in court.
hint2: A good liar's story sounds like this.
hint3: Lots of clear evidence makes an essay this.
hint4: 'Her argument is so ___ that I now agree with her.'

hint1: Weather forecasters say it a lot.
hint2: You think it will happen, but you are not 100% certain.
hint3: Stronger than 'might', weaker than 'definitely'.
hint4: 'Look at those dark clouds. It will ___ rain soon.'

hint1: Scientists use it so they don't sound too certain.
hint2: Like 'can' or 'will', it comes before a base verb.
hint3: 'The results ___ be different in other countries.'
hint4: It is also the name of a month in spring.

hint1: Writers use it when they are far from certain.
hint2: 'Take an umbrella. It ___ rain later.'
hint3: Weaker than 'probably': there is some chance, but not much.
hint4: As a noun, it means great power: 'with all her ___'.

hint1: Use it to say what you expect to happen.
hint2: With dark clouds overhead, rain is this.
hint3: Better than 50-50, but not 100%.
hint4: 'Prices are ___ to rise next year.'

hint1: Researchers use it to describe a pattern, not a rule.
hint2: Softer than 'always'; it leaves room for exceptions.
hint3: It says what happens most of the time.
hint4: 'I ___ sleep late at weekends; most Saturdays, I wake up at ten.'

hint1: Scientists use it when the evidence is not complete yet.
hint2: Like saying 'from what I can tell...'
hint3: Judging only by what you can observe, without proof.
hint4: 'The students ___ enjoy the new timetable: they're all smiling.'

hint1: Sherlock Holmes does this all the time.
hint2: Readers do it when a writer hints but never says.
hint3: Speakers suggest; listeners do this.
hint4: 'We can ___ from his shaking hands that he is afraid.'

hint1: A raised eyebrow or a long silence can do this.
hint2: Writers do it so readers must read between the lines.
hint3: The writer does this; the reader then works it out.
hint4: 'I'm not calling you lazy! I didn't mean to ___ that.'

hint1: Colour, music and body language can all do this.
hint2: It carries a feeling or idea from writer to reader.
hint3: 'The short sentences ___ a sense of panic.'
hint4: Related to the moving belt at a supermarket checkout.

hint1: Films can do this to a group fairly or unfairly.
hint2: Media studies asks how the news does this to teenagers.
hint3: 'The writer ___ the father as caring but strict.'
hint4: What an actor does with a real person, or a painter with a face.

hint1: Repetition in a speech often does this.
hint2: Saying one word louder than the rest does it.
hint3: Bold type and capital letters do this on a page.
hint4: What a bright yellow pen does to key words in your notes.

hint1: Often paired with a similar command word in essay titles.
hint2: Writers do this with a noisy street and a silent house.
hint3: Only the gaps between two things matter, not what they share.
hint4: On a TV or computer screen, it's the setting next to brightness.

hint1: Historians try to consider more than one.
hint2: In a first-person story, you get only the narrator's.
hint3: The same war looks different to a soldier and to a general.
hint4: 'The story is told from a child's ___.'

hint1: Formal emails and chats with friends need different ones.
hint2: It can be angry, playful, formal or sarcastic.
hint3: How a piece of writing sounds to the reader.
hint4: Saying 'another brilliant idea' after a mistake creates a sarcastic ___.

hint1: Teachers often praise a good one, even when marks are low.
hint2: Rolling your eyes in class shows a bad one.
hint3: What a person thinks about something, shown by how they behave.
hint4: 'She has a very negative ___ towards homework.'

hint1: Examiners only give marks for points that are this.
hint2: Pandas in an essay about cars? That fact is not this.
hint3: Stick to what the question asks; don't wander off-topic.
hint4: 'Choose a quotation that is ___ to your argument.'

hint1: Exam instructions should always be this.
hint2: A 'No Smoking' sign leaves nothing for you to work out.
hint3: Put into plain words, so nobody has to guess.
hint4: 'The notice gives an ___ warning: Danger, keep out!'

hint1: Good detectives and careful readers notice these messages.
hint2: A sigh from your parent can carry this kind of criticism.
hint3: 'There was an ___ threat in his smile, though he said nothing.'
hint4: Understood without ever being said out loud.

hint1: Teachers want more of this and less description.
hint2: TV football experts give one after the match, with replays.
hint3: A close look at each part of a text and how it works.
hint4: The noun for taking a text apart to show how it works.

hint1: You write it on a test paper.
hint2: Put your hand up if you know it.
hint3: The teacher asks, and you give this.
hint4: What is 2 + 2? The ___ is 4.

hint1: Artists and detectives look for these.
hint2: Good stories are full of them: the colour of a coat, a smell.
hint3: Something tiny you only see if you look carefully.
hint4: 'One ___ in the photo is the ring on her finger.'

hint1: A poem can have more than one.
hint2: Red in a picture can carry this: love, danger or anger.
hint3: Not what you see, but what it tells you.
hint4: 'I don't know this word. What is its ___?'

hint1: Every advert, poster and website has one.
hint2: To sell, to inform, to entertain or to persuade.
hint3: The job a text was made to do.
hint4: 'The ___ of this advert is to sell perfume.'

hint1: Comments under a YouTube video show it.
hint2: Laughing or crying at a film are examples.
hint3: Not to a question: to a film, song or advert.
hint4: 'The advert got a very angry ___ from viewers.'

hint1: Film-makers make hundreds of these for every film.
hint2: Tea or coffee? Now you have to make one.
hint3: Setting a story in a city, not on a beach, is one.
hint4: 'I had no ___. I had to do it.'

hint1: News reports do this to politicians, kindly or harshly.

hint3: 'The article tries to ___ the team as heroes.'
hint4: Same spelling as what you unwrap on your birthday.

hint1: Artists, writers and chefs all do this.
hint2: Minecraft players can do this with blocks.

hint4: 'The music and lighting ___ a tense atmosphere.'

hint1: Brave adverts do this to old ideas.

hint3: Say 'that's not always true' to a common belief.
hint4: Also a noun: a hard task, like a TikTok dance ___.

hint1: Armies send extra soldiers to do this to a weak position.

hint3: Like emphasise, but for beliefs the audience already holds.

hint1: Dolphins and bees can do this too.
hint2: Emojis let you do this without writing words.

hint4: Phones, letters and sign language all help people do this.

hint4: 'The advert ___ parents by showing a happy, safe family.'

hint1: Bright colours help a poster title do this.

hint3: A red apple in a box of green ones does this.
hint4: 'Her bright pink hair makes her ___ in a crowd.'

hint1: Clear headings do this for the reader of a long report.

hint4: Also a person who shows tourists around a city.

hint1: Busy students must learn to do this with homework.

hint4: Put the most urgent task at the top of your to-do list.
